name: Dinesh
definition: Dinesh is a composite portrait of a Vokkaliga pepper-curing unit supervisor living in Thirthahalli taluk, Shivamogga district, in the Malnad region. He represents families who bridge plantation and processing work, earning modest but regular incomes while facing the pressure of ghat-road disruptions, youth outmigration and the uncertainties of crop prices.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Dinesh works at a small pepper-curing unit on the edge of Thirthahalli town, where black pepper harvested from estates across the taluk arrives for drying, grading and packing. His day begins at seven in the morning, checking the boiling vats and drying racks, supervising three labourers who turn the berries on concrete floors under the sun. During peak season from December to February he works ten-hour days, coordinating lorry loads from estates in Hosanagara and Sringeri taluks and ensuring each batch meets the grade buyers in Mangaluru demand. His monthly salary is around fourteen thousand rupees, with a small bonus at year-end if the unit meets its target. Income is stable compared to daily farm labour but far below what estate owners earn. Monsoon months bring lighter loads and shorter hours; he uses that time to help his brother repair their family's small areca garden. Pepper prices swung wildly in recent years—peaks near six hundred rupees per kilogram followed by crashes to three hundred—and that volatility trickles down: when prices fall, the unit owner delays bonuses and talks of cutting shifts. Dinesh keeps an eye on Coffee Board bulletins and trader gossip, knowing his livelihood hinges on crop cycles he does not control.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Dinesh lives in a tile-roofed house in a Vokkaliga-majority neighbourhood a kilometre from the curing unit, sharing the compound with his wife Suma, their two children, his widowed mother and his unmarried younger brother. Suma works part-time as a tailor from home, stitching blouses and school uniforms for neighbours, adding three to four thousand rupees a month to the household budget. Their elder child, a daughter aged sixteen, is in second PUC at the government junior college in Thirthahalli town; their son, thirteen, attends eighth standard at the nearby high school. Dinesh's mother, now seventy, manages the kitchen and the small vegetable patch behind the house. His brother drives an auto-rickshaw on the Thirthahalli-Sringeri route and contributes to household expenses. Dinesh's father died eight years ago, leaving a half-acre areca garden that the brothers now maintain together, hiring labour for the annual harvest. Household decisions—what to plant, whether to repair the roof, how much to spend on the daughter's college fees—are made collectively over evening tea. Suma's earnings give her a voice in those discussions, though Dinesh's salary remains the anchor. Gender roles are conventional: Suma cooks, cleans and sews, Dinesh handles outside work and dealings with the unit owner, but the line blurs when harvest or festival demands call everyone into the garden.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Dinesh completed his SSLC in 1998 at the government high school in Thirthahalli, then worked for two years before attempting first PUC; he dropped out after failing twice, unable to manage studies alongside wage work his family needed. He learned pepper-curing on the job, starting as a labourer and rising to supervisor over fifteen years. His children's schooling is the household's clearest aspiration. His daughter travels three kilometres by KSRTC bus to the junior college every morning, studying the science stream with hopes of a nursing diploma or a BSc; the family spends around two thousand rupees per month on her college fees, textbooks and bus fare under the Shakti free-ride scheme, which helps but does not cover private tuition she takes for physics and chemistry. His son's school is closer, fees are nominal, but Dinesh worries about the boy's attention—he is more interested in his uncle's auto than in homework. The family hopes the daughter will finish PUC, secure a seat in a nursing college in Shivamogga or Manipal, and earn a steady job. Dinesh knows that path requires money they barely have; a government nursing seat costs upwards of fifty thousand rupees for three years, and private seats are out of reach. He has no savings earmarked for it yet.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Dinesh's health is generally sound, though he has begun to feel joint pain in his knees from years of standing on concrete floors, and a persistent cough from inhaling pepper dust during peak-season boiling and drying. He avoids doctors unless the pain becomes unbearable; a visit to the government taluk hospital in Thirthahalli costs him a lost day's wages. His mother has diabetes and high blood pressure, managed with tablets from the primary health centre, but the family spent eight thousand rupees last year when she needed an ECG and specialist consultation at McGann Hospital in Shivamogga town, a two-hour bus ride away. His daughter had dengue two monsoons ago, requiring a week's hospitalisation at a private clinic in Thirthahalli; the bill came to eighteen thousand rupees, borrowed from a self-help-group contact of Suma's and still being repaid. The household's main health anxieties are twofold: the cost of any serious illness that the government hospital cannot handle, and the seasonal risk of waterborne disease in the monsoon when the well water turns cloudy. Dinesh knows families in forest-fringe villages near Sringeri who lost members to Kyasanur Forest Disease and snakebite, but Thirthahalli town feels removed from that; still, every January when KFD cases appear in the newspapers, his mother mutters prayers. No one in the household is covered by health insurance; Dinesh applied for Ayushman Bharat but his card has not arrived. Suma's tailoring gives her chronic neck and eye strain; she refuses to spend money on spectacles.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Dinesh's family is Vokkaliga, the dominant landowning community across much of Hassan and southern Shivamogga, though Thirthahalli's population also includes Havyaka Brahmins tied to the areca economy, Kurubas, Scheduled Castes, a small Muslim trading community and migrant labourers from north Karnataka and Odisha who work the estates. Dinesh attends the Rama temple near the taluk office for major festivals—Ugadi, Dasara—and his mother insists on a daily lamp at the household shrine. The family observes Sankranti with sugarcane and sesame sweets, and his mother makes a pilgrimage to Sringeri Sharada Peetham every two years. Community ties are dense: Dinesh's neighbours are mostly Vokkaliga families he has known since childhood, and mutual aid—borrowing rice, lending a vehicle for a wedding, helping with harvest labour—is routine. Suma's self-help group, linked to a local NGO and SKDRDP credit, meets twice a month; it is as much a social institution as a financial one, a space where women discuss children's schooling and arbitrate neighbourhood disputes. Caste surfaces in marriage alliances and in the unspoken preference for Vokkaliga tenants when his brother considers renting out a room, but day-to-day interactions at the curing unit, in the market and on the bus are functionally caste-blind. Dinesh is proud of Kuvempu's Thirthahalli connection and of the Keladi Nayaka heritage taught in school, though he admits he has never visited the Keladi museum.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: He accessed the Vidya Nidhi scholarship scheme to help cover his daughter's first-year PUC fees but found the disbursement delayed by four months, forcing him to borrow short-term. Suma's self-help group helped her secure a small loan to buy a sewing machine, and Dinesh credits SKDRDP for being more reliable than the taluk panchayat office, where clerks demand repeat visits for simple certificates. The household does not qualify for a BPL card—Dinesh's salary pushes them just above the line—so they miss ration-shop subsidies and are ineligible for some housing and health schemes. Dinesh's most direct government interaction is the ESI dispensary at the curing unit, which provides basic medicines but nothing more. He has never attended a gram sabha, seeing it as the domain of landed farmers, but he joined a small roadside protest last year when the Thirthahalli-Sringeri road remained unrepaired through the monsoon, blocking pepper and coffee lorries for weeks. He expects little from officials unless pressure is applied collectively. The September 2026 legislature resolution on the Kasturirangan ESA, which he read about in Prajavani, reassured him that farm and plantation land would be protected, but he remains wary of any notification from Bengaluru that could redraw boundaries or restrict his brother's areca garden.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Dinesh is proud to live in Thirthahalli, the taluk that gave Karnataka Kuvempu, and he takes quiet satisfaction in the greenness of Malnad, the reliability of the monsoon and the quality of the pepper and coffee that pass through his hands. But that pride coexists with a constant, low-grade anxiety about money and the future. His daughter's PUC fees and the dream of a nursing seat loom large; he calculates and recalculates what he can save, knowing it will not be enough. He resents the way Bengaluru and the coast get highways, airports and medical colleges while Malnad roads wash out every monsoon and the nearest decent hospital is two hours away. The Kasturirangan ESA notification, though softened by the September resolution, still feels like a threat—one more rule from the city that ignores how families like his make a living. At the same time, he blames estate owners and traders for squeezing labour and keeping wages low while pepper and coffee prices soar. He demands better roads, local colleges, job schemes for youth and reliable health clinics. He wants his children to have the choices he did not, and he fears they will leave the moment they do.
